text:
B: Hello. Good afternoon. Can you see me?
A: Yeah, I can see you, mate. Darren. You alright?
B: I am Tomasz. Yes, I am fine, thank you. Not too bad.
A: Where's that to then, where are you?
B: Sorry?
A: Sorry, where are you based, like?
B: Ah. Crawley, in West Sussex. Near Gatwick. And you?
A: Bridgwater, Somerset. Down the M5. Bit quieter than Gatwick, I reckon.
B: Yes, the planes are noisy when the wind changes. You get used to it. Mostly.
A: Ha. I had that puzzle thing at the start, did you do that? Proper did my head in, that did.
B: Yes. I finished most of them. The last one I am not sure if it was correct.
A: Most of them? Blimey. I got about half, I reckon. Not my sort of thing, puzzles. What d'you do for work then?
B: Er, at the moment I am not working. I was a civil engineer, drainage and highways design, for a consultancy near Gatwick. They made a restructure in the beginning of last year and I was made redundant. So now I am applying for jobs.
A: Oh, sorry to hear that, mate. That's rough.
B: It is okay. The company had to cut, somebody had to go. I keep a spreadsheet of every application, so I am, how do you say, organised about it at least.
A: More organised than me, I'll tell you that. I do cleaning, part-time, at a supermarket. Three early shifts a week. Up at half four, so I'm knackered by about two o'clock. I used to do warehouse stuff, forklift and that, but my back and my knee put a stop to it, sort of thing.
B: I understand. I have also a back condition. The physio told me to walk every day, so I walk one hour in Tilgate Park. It helps.
A: Yeah? I walk the dog along the river, the Parrett. Tyson, he's a Staffie, getting on a bit now, so it's more of a stroll than a walk, d'you know what I mean. We're both slowing down.
B: Ha. Yes. It is the same for everybody.
A: What's your missus do, if you don't mind me asking?
B: My wife is a senior care assistant, in a residential home.
A: You're joking. So's mine. Karen. Care assistant at a home, nearly full-time. Long old shifts, she does.
B: Really? That is a coincidence. Yes, it is hard work. Agnieszka comes home very tired. And the weekends also.
A: Proper hard. I feel a bit bad sometimes, honestly, she's doing all them hours and I'm doing my three mornings. But there you go.
B: I think you do what your body allows. It is honest work. That is what matters, I would say.
A: Yeah. Cheers, mate. Yeah. So what d'you do with yourself, now you're not working?
B: The garden, mainly. I have a greenhouse with tomatoes, and this year they are doing very well. And I fix things. Last week I fixed the gate of my neighbour.
A: Oh, you're handy then. I've got a moped in my shed I've been doing up. Six years, mind. It's nearly finished.
B: Six years. Then it must be very good when it is finished.
A: Ha, that's one way of putting it. Karen reckons I just go out there to get away from the telly.
B: That is also a good reason for a shed, I think.
A: Exactly, mate. You get it. Do you have kids?
B: Two. My son is an electrician in Horsham, and my daughter is a pharmacist in Brighton. They have left home, so it is only us now. And sometimes my daughter's cat.
A: Same, two grown-up. My daughter's in Bristol, she's got a little one, so I'm a grandad now. That's her in the photo behind me, actually.
B: Ah, yes, I saw the photo. Congratulations. That is—
